title: Many ways to measure distance
objectives: Compare Euclidean, taxicab and maximum metrics, and draw their unit balls.

screens.title: Exactly one block away
screens.prose: A taxi in a grid city drives only east-west and north-south. Its distance from the origin is $|x| + |y|$, the **taxicab** distance. Eight points sit round the origin.
screens.question: Tap every point at taxicab distance exactly 1 from the origin.

hints.text: Add the sizes of the two coordinates, ignoring signs.
Four points give exactly 1. $(0.6, 0.8)$ gives 1.4, $(1, 1)$ gives 2.

feedback.correct: Right. Four points, and they do not lie on a circle.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $|x| + |y|$ for each point.

byKey.p5: $(0.6, 0.8)$ is 1 away in a straight line. By taxi it is $0.6 + 0.8 = 1.4$.
byKey.p6: $(1, 1)$ has its larger coordinate equal to 1. The taxicab sum is 2.
byKey.p3: You missed $(-0.3, 0.7)$: signs do not count, so it is $0.3 + 0.7 = 1$.

explain.text: The four points with $|x| + |y| = 1$ lie on a diamond with corners on the axes. $(0.6, 0.8)$ lies on the circle instead, and $(1, 1)$ on the square.

screens.title: Trace the taxicab circle
screens.prose: Drag $P$. Its trail stays on screen, and the caption gives three distances from the origin. Keep $d_1 = 1$ as you go.
screens.question: Drag $P$ to a point with $d_1(0, P) = 1$ in the third quadrant, where both coordinates are negative.

hints.text: Both coordinates negative, sizes adding to 1.

feedback.correct: Right. The trail in every quadrant is a straight edge.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep both coordinates negative and $|x| + |y| = 1$.

explain.text: In the third quadrant $|x| + |y| = 1$ is the line $x + y = -1$. The four edges make the diamond, the taxicab unit circle.

screens.title: Three distances, recalled
screens.prose: Recall `analysis` l22. A metric is never negative, is zero exactly when the points are equal, is symmetric and obeys the triangle inequality. Its unit balls were the circle ($d_2$), the diamond ($d_1$) and the square ($d_\infty$).
screens.question: Fill in the three distances from $(0, 0)$ to $(2, 1)$. Give $d_2$ to four decimal places.

hints.text: The gaps are 2 and 1.
Straight line, sum of gaps, larger gap.
$\sqrt5 \approx 2.2361$, then 3, then 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the gaps 2 and 1 in each formula.

byKey.nosqrt: You gave $2^2 + 1^2 = 5$ without the square root.

explain.text: $d_2 = \sqrt5 \approx 2.2361$, $d_1 = 3$ and $d_\infty = 2$. The order $d_\infty \le d_2 \le d_1$ is no accident; we prove it shortly.

screens.title: A whole family of balls
screens.prose: For $p \ge 1$ put $d_p(x, y) = (|x_1 - y_1|^p + |x_2 - y_2|^p)^{1/p}$. Then $p = 1$ is taxicab and $p = 2$ is Euclidean. Slide $p$ and watch the unit ball $\{y : d_p(0, y) < 1\}$.
screens.question: Set $p = 4$. What area does the unit ball enclose? Read it from the caption.

hints.text: Move the slider to 4.0 and read the caption.
The caption shows about 3.7081.

feedback.correct: Right. The ball fills more of the square as $p$ grows.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Set the slider to exactly 4.0.

byKey.square: 4 is the square $[-1, 1]^2$, the limit as $p$ grows. At $p = 4$ the corners are still rounded.
byKey.circle: $\pi$ is the disc at $p = 2$. Move the slider on to 4.

explain.text: The area is 2 at $p = 1$, $\pi \approx 3.1416$ at $p = 2$, about 3.5333 at $p = 3$ and 3.7081 at $p = 4$. As $p \to \infty$, $d_p \to d_\infty$ and the ball tends to the square of area 4.

screens.title: Why the distances come in order
screens.prose: We prove $d_\infty \le d_2 \le d_1 \le 2d_\infty$ for any two points of the plane. Three middle lines may come in any order. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Write $a = |x_1 - y_1|$ and $b = |x_2 - y_2|$; both are at least 0.
$d_\infty = \max(a, b) = \sqrt{\max(a, b)^2} \le \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = d_2$, since one square is at most the sum of both.
$d_2^2 = a^2 + b^2 \le a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = d_1^2$, since $ab \ge 0$; take square roots.
$d_1 = a + b \le 2\max(a, b) = 2d_\infty$, since each of $a$ and $b$ is at most the larger.
So $d_\infty \le d_2 \le d_1 \le 2d_\infty$ for every pair of points. $\blacksquare$
Check $(0, 0)$ and $(2, 1)$: $2 \le 2.2361 \le 3 \le 4$, so the chain holds.
lines.why: One pair of points is an example, not a proof. The claim is for every pair, so it needs the algebra.

hints.text: Name the two gaps first, and conclude last.
Each middle line proves one link of the chain.

feedback.correct: Right. Each link has its own one-line reason.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Start by naming the gaps; end with the chain.

byKey.d1: You used one example as the proof. A check on $(2, 1)$ cannot cover every pair.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the example line is flawed.

explain.text: Take $a, b \ge 0$. One square is at most the sum, $2ab \ge 0$, and each gap is at most the larger. So $d_\infty \le d_2 \le d_1 \le 2d_\infty$.

screens.title: The balls nest
screens.prose: The chain of inequalities nests the balls round the origin. A smaller distance lets more points in, so its ball is larger.

state.caption: Four balls round the origin: two squares, a diamond and a circle.

screens.question: Order the four open balls from smallest to largest.

hints.text: Use $d_1 \le 2d_\infty$ for the first link.
The small square sits inside the diamond.
Then $d_2 \le d_1$ and $d_\infty \le d_2$ give the next two links.

feedback.correct: Right. Each inclusion is one link of the chain.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A point in a smaller ball must lie in the next one.

byKey.d: The big square is the largest, since $d_\infty \le d_2$ lets every disc point in.

explain.text: If $d_\infty < \tfrac12$ then $d_1 < 1$; if $d_1 < 1$ then $d_2 < 1$; if $d_2 < 1$ then $d_\infty < 1$. So $B_\infty(0, \tfrac12) \subseteq B_1(0, 1) \subseteq B_2(0, 1) \subseteq B_\infty(0, 1)$.

screens.title: The largest disc in the diamond
screens.prose: Shrink the disc $B_2(0, r)$ until it fits inside the diamond $B_1(0, 1)$.
screens.question: What is the largest $r$ with $B_2(0, r) \subseteq B_1(0, 1)$? Give four decimal places.

widget.accept: 0.7071: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, the distance from 0 to the line $x + y = 1$.

hints.text: The disc first touches an edge, not a corner.
The nearest point of the edge $x + y = 1$ is $(0.5, 0.5)$.
Its distance from 0 is $\sqrt{0.5^2 + 0.5^2}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the Euclidean distance from 0 to the nearest edge.

byKey.one: Radius 1 reaches the corners, but the disc pokes out near $(0.7, 0.7)$, where $d_1 = 1.4$.
byKey.half: $\tfrac12$ is the half-size square that fits. A disc of radius $\tfrac12$ still has room.

explain.text: The edge $x + y = 1$ is nearest the origin at $(0.5, 0.5)$, at distance $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.7071$. The largest $r$ with $B_\infty(0, r) \subseteq B_2(0, 1)$ is also $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, by the corner $(r, r)$.

screens.title: Three balls in space
screens.prose: In $\mathbb{R}^3$ the unit balls are an octahedron ($d_1$), a sphere ($d_2$) and a cube ($d_\infty$). Step through them with the first control. Move $P$ with the others.

derive.caption: $P$ = ({{fixed(a, 2)}}, {{fixed(b, 2)}}, {{fixed(c, 2)}}): $d_1$ = {{fixed(abs(a) + abs(b) + abs(c), 3)}}, $d_2$ = {{fixed(sqrt(a*a + b*b + c*c), 3)}}, $d_\infty$ = {{fixed(max(abs(a), abs(b), abs(c)), 3)}}

screens.question: Which open unit balls contain $P = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5)$? Select all that apply.

hints.text: Read the three distances in the caption.
Step to the octahedron and turn the view.

feedback.correct: Right. Inside the sphere and cube, outside the octahedron.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare each distance with 1.

explain.text: $d_1 = 1.5$, $d_2 = \sqrt{0.75} \approx 0.8660$ and $d_\infty = 0.5$. The volumes are $\tfrac43$, $\tfrac{4\pi}{3} \approx 4.1888$ and 8, nested as in the plane. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ the constants become $d_1 \le \sqrt n\, d_2$ and $d_2 \le \sqrt n\, d_\infty$.

screens.title: Bigger distances, bigger ball?
screens.prose: A learner reasons: "The taxicab metric gives the biggest distances of the three. So its unit ball must be the biggest."
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: The taxicab ball is the smallest: a larger distance leaves fewer points within 1.
The taxicab ball is the biggest, since its distances are the biggest.
options.why: You carried "bigger distance" over to "bigger ball". It runs the other way: $(0.6, 0.6)$ has $d_1 = 1.2$, so it is outside.

options.text: The taxicab ball is the square $[-1, 1]^2$, like a grid of streets.
options.why: You drew the streets, not the distance. The corner $(1, 1)$ is taxicab distance 2; the square is the $d_\infty$ ball.

options.text: All three balls are the same size, since all have radius 1.
options.why: The radius is the same, but each metric measures it differently. $(0.6, 0.6)$ is in two balls and not the third.

hints.text: Is $(0.6, 0.6)$ within 1 of the origin in each metric?
Its taxicab distance is 1.2.
Larger distances exclude more points, so the ball shrinks.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Test the point $(0.6, 0.6)$ in each metric.

byKey.big: You took bigger distances to mean a bigger ball. Bigger distances let fewer points within 1, so the ball is smaller.

explain.text: Since $d_1 \ge d_2 \ge d_\infty$, the condition $d_1 < 1$ is the hardest to meet. So the diamond sits inside the circle, which sits inside the square.

screens.title: Below p = 1
screens.prose: The formula for $d_p$ still makes sense at $p = 0.5$. Take the points $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$.
screens.question: What is $d_{0.5}\big((0, 0), (1, 1)\big) = (1^{0.5} + 1^{0.5})^{2}$?

feedback.correct: Right. And each leg via $(1, 0)$ has length 1.

byKey.nopow: You added $1 + 1 = 2$ but did not raise to the power $1/p = 2$.
byKey.root: You took a square root at the end. The outer power is $1/p = 2$, a square.

explain.text: The direct distance is 4, but via $(1, 0)$ the two legs give $1 + 1 = 2$. So $4 > 2$ breaks the triangle inequality: $d_{0.5}$ is not a metric. Its ball is a non-convex star of area $\tfrac23$.

screens.title: Distances by machine
screens.prose: Write `dist(x, y, p)` for tuples of any length, with `p = math.inf` giving the maximum metric. Raise `ValueError` when `p < 1`, since that is no metric. Then write `nearest(points, q, p)`: the index of the point nearest `q`, the first on a tie.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. Distances use math.isclose (relative 1e-9); indices and the ValueError are compared exactly. The first Check starts Python in the browser, which takes about 4 s once.

hints.text: Build the list of coordinate gaps first.
For `math.inf` return the largest gap; otherwise sum the $p$-th powers and take the $1/p$ power.

feedback.correct: Right. The nearest point changes with the metric.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the maximum case and the error for small $p$.

explain.text: In $d_2$, $A = (3, 0)$ and $B = (2, 2)$ are 3 and 2.8284 from 0; in $d_\infty$, 3 and 2. So $B$ is nearer. In $d_1$ they are 3 against 4, so $A$ wins.

screens.title: Rebalancing a portfolio
screens.prose: A £2m portfolio moves from weights $(0.40, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10)$ to $(0.25, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15)$. Each metric answers a desk question: total traded, the largest single trade, a tracking-style gap.
screens.question: Fill in the three distances between the weight vectors. Give $d_2$ to four decimal places.

hints.text: Use the Change column, ignoring signs.
The largest change is asset 1.

feedback.correct: Right. £600,000 traded, at most £300,000 in one name.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work from the sizes of the four changes.

byKey.net: You added the signed changes, which always cancel to 0. Turnover adds the sizes.

explain.text: $d_1 = 0.30$ is £600,000 traded and $d_\infty = 0.15$ is a £300,000 trade in asset 1. A turnover limit is a $d_1$ ball and a per-name limit a $d_\infty$ ball; $d_2 = \sqrt{0.03} \approx 0.1732$. Matching today's market to its nearest day in history can change its answer with the metric, as `nearest` showed.

ideas: The $d_p$ distances $(|x_1 - y_1|^p + |x_2 - y_2|^p)^{1/p}$ are metrics for $p \ge 1$; $p = 1$ is taxicab, $p = 2$ Euclidean, and $p \to \infty$ gives the maximum.

In the plane $d_\infty \le d_2 \le d_1 \le 2d_\infty$, so the balls nest: $B_\infty(0, \tfrac12) \subseteq B_1(0, 1) \subseteq B_2(0, 1) \subseteq B_\infty(0, 1)$. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ the constants are $\sqrt n$ and $n$.
For $p < 1$ the formula breaks the triangle inequality: $d_{0.5}((0, 0), (1, 1)) = 4 > 1 + 1$.

formula.name: The chain of metrics in the plane
formula.note: For every pair of points. Larger distances give smaller balls.

summary.trap: The taxicab metric gives the largest distances, so its unit ball is the smallest, not the largest.

quiz.prose: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ we have $d_2 \le d_1$, and also $d_1 \le c\, d_2$ for some constant $c$.
quiz.question: What is the best constant $c$?

options.why: $n$ is the constant in $d_1 \le n\, d_\infty$. Against $d_2$, Cauchy-Schwarz gives $\sqrt n$.
You used the plane's $d_1 \le 2d_\infty$. Against $d_2$ the plane's constant is $\sqrt2$, and it grows with $n$.

feedback.correct: Right. Equality at the all-ones vector.

explain.text: By Cauchy-Schwarz, $\sum |a_k| \le \sqrt n \sqrt{\sum a_k^2}$. At $(1, \dots, 1)$, $d_1 = n$ and $d_2 = \sqrt n$, so $\sqrt n$ cannot be lowered.

quiz.prose: A square $B_\infty(0, r)$ sits inside the diamond $B_1(0, 1)$.
quiz.question: What is the largest such $r$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The square's corner $(r, r)$ must have $d_1 \le 1$.

byKey.root: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ is the disc that fits. The square's corners stick out further.

explain.text: The corner $(r, r)$ has $d_1 = 2r$, so we need $2r \le 1$, giving $r = 0.5$. This is the link $d_1 \le 2d_\infty$ again.

quiz.question: Which point lies in $B_2(0, 1)$ but not in $B_1(0, 1)$?

options.why: $d_1 = 0.7$, so it lies in both balls.
$d_2 = 1$ exactly, and the open ball needs $< 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compute $d_2$ and $d_1$ for each.

explain.text: $(0.6, 0.6)$ has $d_2 = \sqrt{0.72} \approx 0.849 < 1$ and $d_1 = 1.2 > 1$. It sits in the disc outside the diamond.

quiz.question: What is $d_3\big((0, 0), (1, 1)\big)$? Give four decimal places.

byKey.d2: That is $d_2 = \sqrt2$. For $p = 3$ take the cube root.
byKey.sum: You added the gaps, which is $d_1$, and stopped before the $1/3$ power.

explain.text: $(1 + 1)^{1/3} = 2^{1/3} \approx 1.2599$. As $p$ grows the value falls from $d_1 = 2$ towards $d_\infty = 1$.
